title: HTTP Fundamentals
shortDescription: A compact course on HTTP request and response basics.

scope.outcome: Explain how HTTP clients and servers exchange requests, responses, methods, headers, and status codes.

content.heading: Explanation
content.value: HTTP is a request-response protocol used by browsers, servers, command-line clients, APIs, and many distributed systems. This section builds on the prerequisite idea that clients ask for resources and servers answer with representations. A client starts an exchange by sending a request that names the desired resource and the action it wants performed. A server answers with a response that includes a status code, metadata, and sometimes a response body. This foundation matters because web developers debug systems by locating where an exchange failed: the request may target the wrong URL, omit required headers, use the wrong method, or send a body the server cannot interpret.

content.heading: Worked example
content.value: Imagine a browser loading a course page. The browser sends an HTTP request for the page URL. The server checks whether the route exists, chooses the resource representation, and returns an HTTP response. A successful response usually includes a status code in the 200 range and headers describing the content type and caching behavior. If the page is missing, the server returns a 404 response instead. The learner should be able to separate the request decision from the response outcome and explain what each side contributes.

content.heading: Practice
content.value: Practice by opening a browser network panel and reloading a page. Pick one request and identify the request URL, method, request headers, response status code, response headers, and response body type. Then write a short diagnosis of what would change if the request used a different method or if the server returned a redirect. This exercise turns HTTP from an abstract protocol into an observable engineering trace.

content.heading: Explanation
content.value: HTTP methods and status codes give shared meaning to web exchanges. This module moves from the foundation of messages to the deeper semantic contract that lets teams reason about API behavior. A method such as GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, or DELETE tells the server what kind of action the client is requesting. A status code tells the client how the server interpreted the request. This vocabulary allows clients, servers, proxies, caches, and developers to coordinate without a private explanation for every endpoint. The exact response body may differ across applications, but the method and status code provide a common diagnostic frame for mastery evidence in quizzes, debugging exercises, and project reviews.

content.heading: Worked example
content.value: Consider a form that creates a new course note. The client might send a POST request to a notes endpoint with a JSON body. If the note is created, the server can return a 201 status. If the submitted JSON is missing a required field, the server might return a 400-level status. If the learner is not signed in, the response may be 401 or 403 depending on the authorization problem. Reading the method and status code together helps identify whether the issue is intent, input, authentication, authorization, or missing resources.

content.heading: Practice
content.value: Practice by describing three API interactions: reading a resource, creating a resource, and handling a missing resource. For each interaction, choose a method, predict a likely success status code, and name one failure status code. Then explain what evidence you would inspect in the request and response to confirm your diagnosis. This creates a habit of using HTTP semantics as engineering evidence rather than memorized trivia.

concepts.name: HTTP method
concepts.description: A request verb that communicates the action the client wants the server to consider.

concepts.name: HTTP status code
concepts.description: A numeric response classification that communicates the outcome of a request.
